subject: History (Social Science)
textbook: Our Pasts — Part I (History Textbook for Class VI)

cards.front: Name the four main types of ancient towns discussed in this chapter.
cards.back: (1) Craft towns — famous for specific crafts that attracted buyers (e.g., Varanasi for silk, Mathura for cotton cloth). (2) Trade towns — on important routes, river confluences, or coastal ports (e.g., Ujjain, Puhar). (3) Religious/pilgrimage towns — grew around temples, stupas, or monasteries (e.g., Bodh Gaya, Shravanabelagola). (4) Royal/administrative towns — capitals of kingdoms (e.g., Rajgir, Vaishali, Pataliputra).
cards.memory_hook: C-T-R-A = Craft, Trade, Religion, Administration. Most real towns had all four roles simultaneously.

cards.front: What were punch-marked coins? What were they made of and what was special about them?
cards.back: Punch-marked coins were ancient India's first widely used currency. Made of silver or copper. Their symbols (sun, moon, elephant, geometric shapes) were punched (stamped) onto them using metal punches — hence the name. Key features: NO writing, NO portraits of rulers, standardised by WEIGHT not shape (irregular in shape). Used from roughly the 6th century BCE. They replaced barter and enabled long-distance trade across the subcontinent.
cards.memory_hook: PUNCH-marked = symbols PUNCHED in. No face, no writing. Weighed, not shaped. Silver or copper. The coin that built ancient India's trade network.

cards.front: What was a shreni? What were its main functions?
cards.back: A shreni was a guild — an organisation of merchants or craftspeople of the same trade. Functions: (1) Maintained quality standards for goods. (2) Fixed prices and wages. (3) Provided welfare for sick/aged members. (4) Resolved internal disputes. (5) Acted as a bank — accepted deposits, paid interest. (6) Made collective donations to religious institutions. Led by a jetthaka (guild chief). Shrenis were the key economic institution of ancient Indian towns.
cards.memory_hook: SHRENI = Shared Responsibility ENterprise. Like a professional cooperative: shared standards, shared welfare, shared banking.

cards.front: What are Jataka stories and why are they valuable to historians?
cards.back: Jatakas are Buddhist stories about the previous births (lives) of the Buddha — there are about 550 such stories. They are valuable to historians because: (1) They are set in real ancient Indian towns and markets. (2) They describe trade routes, merchant journeys, craft activities, and social life in detail. (3) They mention specific crafts, towns, and economic practices. They are a religious text AND a historical source — but must be cross-checked with other evidence. They describe a monetised, trading economy of ancient India.
cards.memory_hook: JATAKA = Journal of Ancient Times And Kingdoms Alike. Stories of the Buddha's past = stories of ancient India's past. Double purpose: religion + history.

cards.front: What is a ringwell? Why is it important to archaeologists?
cards.back: A ringwell is a structure made by stacking large terracotta (baked clay) rings vertically in a pit in the ground. Used for: wells (accessing groundwater), drainage/soakage pits (for waste water), and storage. Archaeological importance: the presence of large numbers of ringwells at a site indicates dense urban settlement — it shows the community needed organised water supply and drainage, a characteristic of a town rather than a village.
cards.memory_hook: RINGWELL = rings stacked like a pipe = urban water/drainage system. Many ringwells = ancient town. It's the ancient equivalent of finding sewer pipes — it marks a city.

cards.front: Who were dasas and karmakaras in ancient towns?
cards.back: Dasas: slaves in ancient India — they had no freedom, were owned by others, and performed domestic or agricultural labour without wages. Karmakaras: hired workers or wage labourers — free people who worked for daily wages. Both groups were among the poorest people in ancient towns. They did the physical work that kept towns running — carrying, cleaning, farming, construction. In contrast to wealthy setthi/shresthis (merchants), dasas and karmakaras had little social power.
cards.memory_hook: DASA = Dependent, no wages (slave). KARMAKARA = worker for KARna (wages). Together they were the labouring poor who built ancient India's wealth for others.

cards.front: Why was Ujjain considered an important town in ancient India?
cards.back: Ujjain (in present-day Madhya Pradesh) was important as a major trade town because of its strategic location at the crossroads of important trade routes — the north-south route and the east-west route both passed through it. It was also a royal capital (capital of the Avanti kingdom, one of the sixteen Mahajanapadas). It was a religious centre too (associated with the deity Mahakaleshwar). Its combination of trade route position + royal capital + religious importance made it one of ancient India's most thriving cities.
cards.memory_hook: UJJAIN = crossroads = everything meets here. North-South + East-West routes = merchants from everywhere. Royal capital + temple = power + religion. Classic ancient thriving town.

cards.front: What was Puhar (Kaveripattinam) and why was it significant?
cards.back: Puhar (also called Kaveripattinam) was a major port town on the east coast of India (Coromandel coast, Tamil Nadu) at the mouth of the Kaveri river. It was one of ancient south India's most important trade ports — ships from Rome, Arabia, and Southeast Asia anchored here. It is described in detail in Tamil literary works like Silappadikaram. It was a busy, cosmopolitan city with warehouses, markets, temples, and a diverse population of traders from different lands.
cards.memory_hook: PUHAR = PORT at mouth of Kaveri. Ships from everywhere. Tamil literature's favourite ancient city. Sea trade = Rome + Arabia + Southeast Asia.

cards.front: Shravanabelagola in Karnataka — what type of ancient town was it, and what is its claim to historical fame?
cards.back: Shravanabelagola (Hassan district, Karnataka) was a major Jain religious and pilgrimage town. Historical significance: (1) It is one of the most sacred Jain sites — associated with the monk Bhadrabahu and the Mauryan emperor Chandragupta Maurya, who is said to have come here in his old age to fast unto death (Jain practice of sallekhana). (2) It houses the 58-foot monolithic statue of Gomateshvara (Bahubali), carved in the 10th century CE — one of the largest free-standing statues in the world. (3) It has been a Jain centre for over 2,000 years.
cards.memory_hook: SHRAVANABELAGOLA = Shravana (Jain deity) + Bela (pond) + Gola (round hill). Two hills, one giant statue, 2,000 years of Jain pilgrimage. Karnataka's most ancient living pilgrimage town.

cards.front: How did punch-marked coins solve the problems of barter?
cards.back: Barter problems: (1) Double coincidence of wants — both parties must want exactly what the other has. (2) No standard measure of value — hard to compare the value of, say, a cow and a pot. (3) Indivisibility — you cannot give half a cow as change. Punch-marked coins solved all three: (1) Coins are universally accepted — no need for the other party to want your specific goods. (2) Standardised by weight — provides a consistent measure of value. (3) Divisible — different coin denominations. This enabled merchants to travel and trade with strangers across long distances.
cards.memory_hook: Barter = 3 problems (coincidence, value, change). Coin = solves all 3. Universal acceptance + standard weight + divisibility = trade revolution.

cards.front: What was a setthi (shreshti) in ancient India?
cards.back: A setthi (also called shreshti in Sanskrit) was a wealthy merchant or banker in ancient India. Setthis were often the most powerful people in towns — they financed large trade expeditions, lent money to other merchants, advised kings on economic matters, and were major donors to Buddhist monasteries, Jain temples, and Hindu shrines. They often led merchant shrenis. The setthi was to an ancient Indian town what a modern billionaire industrialist is to a city — economically dominant and socially influential.
cards.memory_hook: SETTHI = 'SET'-thi = all SET with wealth. The ancient Indian town's banker-merchant-leader. Rich enough to build monasteries, advise kings, and lead guilds.

cards.front: Why did ancient towns often grow near rivers or on important trade routes?
cards.back: Rivers provided: (1) Water for drinking, agriculture, and crafts. (2) Transport — goods could be moved by boat more cheaply than by cart. (3) Fish — a food source. (4) Fertile land nearby — food for the town's population. Trade routes provided: (1) Flow of merchants bringing goods and money. (2) Demand for services — inns, food, repairs, guides. (3) Security — established routes had rest stops and protection. Towns at the junction of a river AND a trade route (like Varanasi, on the Ganga and on the north-south route) became especially powerful.
cards.memory_hook: River = water + transport + food. Trade route = merchants + money + demand. Junction of both = thriving town guaranteed.

cards.front: Why did merchants donate so much money to Buddhist monasteries and Jain temples?
cards.back: Several reasons: (1) Religious merit — both Buddhism and Jainism taught that donations earn spiritual merit and better rebirths. (2) Social prestige — a merchant who donated a hall to a monastery gained respect and social status in the town. (3) Practical networking — monasteries and temples were centres where merchants gathered, so donating created goodwill among the community. (4) Safe storage — monasteries sometimes stored valuables for merchants. Shreni (guild) inscriptions at Buddhist sites like Sanchi and Bharhut record collective donations — the shreni got its name carved as a group, gaining community prestige.
cards.memory_hook: Merchants donated for 3 reasons: Merit (spiritual), Status (social), Network (practical). MSN = Merchants' Smart Networking through donation.

cards.front: Aihole in Karnataka is called the 'cradle of Indian temple architecture'. What type of ancient town was it?
cards.back: Aihole (Bagalkot district, Karnataka) was primarily a craft and religious town during the Chalukya period (6th–8th century CE). It has over 125 temples built in various experimental styles — the Chalukyan architects used Aihole as a laboratory to develop temple architecture styles that later spread across India. It was also an active trade town on the banks of the Malaprabha river. It combines craft (temple building — a skilled craft), religion (temples), and trade (river route) — a classic multi-purpose ancient town.
cards.memory_hook: AIHOLE = Ancient India's HOLEs in stone (temples). 125+ temples = craftspeople's workshop. 'Cradle of temple architecture' = where Indian temple style was born.

cards.front: What were the sixteen Mahajanapadas and how are they connected to ancient towns?
cards.back: Mahajanapadas were the sixteen large kingdoms and republics of ancient India that flourished from roughly the 6th century BCE. They are listed in Buddhist and Jain texts. Their capitals were the most important towns of the period — examples: Magadha (capital Rajgir, later Pataliputra), Vajji (capital Vaishali), Avanti (capital Ujjain), Kosala (capital Shravasti), Kuru (capital Hastinapura). The Mahajanapadas competed with each other politically and economically — this competition drove the growth of their capitals as fortified, resourceful towns.
cards.memory_hook: MAHA-janapadas = GREAT-kingdoms. 16 kingdoms = 16 great capitals = 16 ancient towns competing for power. Magadha eventually won — becoming the Mauryan Empire.

cards.front: What evidence do historians use to know about ancient towns?
cards.back: Historians use multiple types of evidence: (1) Archaeological excavations — finding ringwells, terracotta artefacts, coins, pottery, building foundations at town sites. (2) Punch-marked coins found at sites confirm trade activity. (3) Inscriptions — donations by shrenis recorded on stone at Buddhist stupas (Sanchi, Bharhut). (4) Literary sources — Jataka stories describe town life; Tamil Sangam literature describes port towns like Puhar. (5) Foreign accounts — Greek ambassador Megasthenes described Pataliputra; Roman writers mentioned Indian ports. Each source type has its limitations — no single source tells the whole story.
cards.memory_hook: A-I-L-F = Archaeology, Inscriptions, Literature, Foreign accounts. Four types of evidence for ancient towns. AILFs = All Important Layers of Finding.

cards.front: How did shrenis function like banks in ancient India?
cards.back: Shrenis performed banking functions by: (1) Accepting deposits — people (including kings and temples) deposited money with a shreni for safekeeping. (2) Paying interest on deposits. (3) Lending money to merchants who needed capital for trade expeditions. (4) Providing letters of credit — allowing merchants to travel without carrying large amounts of coin (they could deposit in one city and collect from the shreni's agent in another). This made shrenis the financial backbone of ancient India's long-distance trade — essentially private banks run by merchant communities.
cards.memory_hook: SHRENI = ancient BANK. Deposits + Interest + Loans + Credit = everything a modern bank does. Ancient India invented banking through the shreni system.

cards.front: Hampi (Vijayanagara) in Karnataka was one of the world's largest cities in the 14th–16th centuries. What type of town was it?
cards.back: Hampi was the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire (present-day Vijayanagara district/Ballari, Karnataka) — it was simultaneously: (1) Royal/administrative capital (seat of the Vijayanagara kings). (2) A major trade town (merchants from Arabia, Portugal, and Southeast Asia traded here; bazaars described by foreign visitors as stretching for miles). (3) A religious centre (city built around the Virupaksha temple complex, still functioning today). (4) A craft centre (master builders, sculptors, weavers). At its peak, Hampi had a population of over 500,000 — one of the world's largest cities.
cards.memory_hook: HAMPI = Huge And Magnificent Place Indeed. Royal + Trade + Religion + Craft = the greatest example of all four types of ancient town combined in one Karnataka city.

cards.front: Why do historians say that towns in ancient India were NOT built by kings alone?
cards.back: Kings built palaces, forts, and sometimes temples — but towns thrived because of many groups working together: (1) Merchants (setthis/shrenis) financed trade, built warehouses, funded religious institutions. (2) Craftspeople produced the goods that made towns famous and prosperous. (3) Ordinary workers (karmakaras, dasas) did the physical labour of construction, agriculture, and service. (4) Religious teachers and pilgrims attracted people to settle near monasteries and temples. (5) Traders from other regions brought foreign goods and ideas. A king's decision to build a capital city created the framework, but the town only thrived when all these groups participated.
cards.memory_hook: Town = King's shell + Merchants' money + Craftspeople's skill + Workers' labour. Remove any one layer and the town collapses. Towns are collective creations.

cards.front: What made Vaishali an important ancient town? What was special about its political system?
cards.back: Vaishali (in present-day Bihar) was the capital of the Vajji confederacy — notable because Vajji was a republic (Gana-Sangha), not a kingdom. Decisions were made by an assembly of representatives, not by a single king. Historical significance: (1) One of the earliest known republics in the world. (2) Important in both Buddhism (the Buddha visited Vaishali and gave some of his last teachings here) and Jainism (Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara, was born near Vaishali). (3) Archaeologically significant — ringwells and other features of ancient town life have been found here. (4) A major trade town on the northern plains route.
cards.memory_hook: VAISHALI = ancient REPUBLIC (not kingdom). Assembly of representatives = early democracy. Also birthplace region of Mahavira + visited by Buddha. Ancient India's democratic city.
